avalancheActivity.comment: In the highest elevations of the High and Western Tatras (above 1,900 m a.s.l.), a MODERATE avalanche danger—Level 2—has developed. The main issue is wind-drifted snow on the leeward sides (W, SE, and NE) of the highest elevations. Be cautious in very steep areas, narrow gullies, slopes below rock walls, and terrain depressions, where snow accumulates in large quantities and forms snow cushions, slabs, and drifts. Prolonged low temperatures and a thin snowpack lead to the development of critical—permanently weak—layers within the snowpack. Avalanches may be triggered primarily by significant additional loading, though the occurrence of smaller spontaneous avalanches from slab snow cannot be ruled out.
avalancheActivity.highlights: Watch out for wind-blown fresh snow on leeward slopes (W, SE, NE)!

snowpackStructure.comment: Following the passage of a cold front, Arctic air has moved into the mountainous regions of Slovakia. In the coming days, we expect light snowfall and continued strong northwesterly winds. Although there is continuous snow cover starting from the foothills, significant snow depth is found only above the tree line, where it reaches 20 to 60 cm, and locally even more. Partly due to low temperatures, the snow layers are not sufficiently bonded together. Due to the wind, the snow cover is distributed unevenly.

avalancheActivity.comment: The main avalanche hazard is fresh, wind-drifted snow on leeward slopes, in gullies, and in hollows, particularly on NE, E, and SE-facing slopes. Strong winds have created snow slabs and pillows in these areas, which can be triggered by added weight and result in small avalanches. Prolonged low temperatures and shallow snow depth are causing critical layers to form within the snowpack.
avalancheActivity.highlights: In the highest elevations of the Low Tatras, there remains a LOW avalanche danger, Level 1.
